predict.ask: You have more than one Python installed. When you type python3, one of them runs. If you use that one to build a virtual environment, which Python is in the environment?
options: The newest one on the machine. A fresh environment should give you a fresh Python.
The one you built it with.
The system one, because that is the real Python and the others are copies.
because: A fresh folder suggests a fresh Python, but section 12.2 of the tutorial says an environment gets “the Python version from which the command was run”. Your pyvenv.cfg shows it: its version line is the version of the Python that made it.
Right. Section 12.2 of the tutorial says an environment gets the Python the command was run with, and your pyvenv.cfg shows it: its version line is the version of the Python that made it.

The Python that comes with macOS can feel like the real one, but an environment does not go looking for a Python. Section 12.2 says it gets the one the command was run with, and the version line of your pyvenv.cfg shows which.

concepts.anchor: Like a folder-specific copy of a tool, rather than a search for the newest tool.
concepts.explain: A virtual environment keeps the Python it was created from. It does not look for a newer one, and it does not look for one that suits this machine better.

concepts.anchor: Like checking drawers in a fixed order and using the first matching tool.
concepts.explain: PATH is an ordered list of folders. The shell looks in them one by one and runs the first match. which python3 names that match, and which -a python3 lists them all.

sessions.title: A loop, its order, and a running total
sessions.subtitle: In this session you write your first loop: it goes through six rows of sales, one at a time, and keeps a running total. In SQL, SUM(amount) added the whole column at once; here you decide where in your code the total starts.

parts.shows: Loop over six rows, count some, keep a running total
parts.why: You write a loop over six rows, few enough to check by eye, that keeps a running total. Watch where you set the total to zero: Python accepts more than one place without an error. A1, this block of sessions, ends with an agent’s script whose weekly total jumped 12% for no business reason, and a loop like this is at its centre.
parts.setup: Six rows are waiting in a file called rows.py; each has a name, a team and an amount. You will fetch the file, write a loop over the rows at the bottom of it, count some of them, and keep a running total until it passes 50. The file stays as it is, so you can check every answer by hand.

predict.ask: These six rows come in a fixed order, and the body of the loop runs once for each row. The body is two lines: first total = 0, then it adds that row’s amount to total. After the sixth row, what does print(total) show?
options: Zero, because it is set to zero again every time through the loop.
because: Adding up is what a total is for, so this is the natural expectation. But total = 0 is inside the loop, so it runs once per row, and each time it wipes what the rows before had added; only the last row’s amount is left. Task 3 is where this shows.
Right. total = 0 runs once per row, so each row starts again from nothing. On these six rows the loop ends at 19, the last amount; with total = 0 set once, before the loop, the same loop ends at 132.

Zero would be right if total = 0 ran after the add. It runs before, so each time through the loop the total is set to zero and then that row’s amount is added, and the loop ends holding the last row’s amount.

rows-read.pass: All six rows went through the loop.
rows-read.fail: Some of the rows never printed. A loop that stops early, or starts at the wrong place, loses rows without saying so.

counted-and-crossed.pass: The sum over 20 is there, and so is the total at the row where it first passed 50.
counted-and-crossed.fail: The sum of the amounts over 20, or the total when it first passed 50, is not here. If nothing ever passes 50, look at where your total is set before you look at anything else.

missing.61: The total at the row where it first passed 50 is not here. If nothing ever passes 50, look at where your total is set before you look at anything else.
missing.83: The sum of the amounts over 20 is not here yet: add up only the rows over 20, and print that sum.

parts.receipt_prompt: Paste your runs — the command, and what came back under it, each time.

compare.note: Where you put total = 0 changes the answer. A plain SUM(amount) works on the whole set at once, with no order; a loop makes you choose where the total starts.

concepts.anchor: Like a running tally on paper: each time you write a new number the old one is gone, and only the last one is there at the end.
concepts.explain: A name holds one value at a time, and assigning to it replaces what was there. The loop body runs once per row of data, so an assignment inside the body runs once per row too.

concepts.anchor: Like a bank statement: the balance on each line depends on every line above it. A SQL SUM has no “above”.
concepts.explain: The rows come in a sequence and a running total depends on it. “Which row did the total first pass 50 at” has no answer without an order.

predict.ask:
Below, bump is handed a number and a list as arguments, and returns nothing. items.append("new") adds an item to the list it is called on.
def bump(number, items):
    number = number + 1
    items.append("new")

count = 1
names = ["Ana"]
bump(count, names)
print(count, names)
What does the last line print?
options: 2 ['Ana', 'new'] — the function changed both of them.
1 ['Ana'] — it changed neither; a function works on its own copies.
1 ['Ana', 'new'] — the list changed and the number did not.
because: Both were handed in, so it is natural to expect both to come back changed. But number = number + 1 only points the function’s own name at a new number, and count outside never sees it. The list is different: append changes the one list that names and items both point to.

Copies would protect both, and this pick expects copies. Python hands over the objects themselves: assigning to number inside moves only the function’s own name, but append changes the very list names points to.
Right. Assigning to number moves only the function’s own name, so count stays 1, while append changes the one list names and items both point to, so the list outside gains the new item.

compare.note: Two things get out of a function: what you return, and any object you changed in place.
compare.after: The two that finished without an error are the costly kind, because nothing warns you. 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact form in binary, so their sum is not 0.30 and the comparison is False; that is why money is kept in whole cents, or in Decimal, not in a float. The column of whole numbers was already at the largest value numpy’s 32-bit whole number can hold (Python’s own whole numbers have no such limit), so adding one made it wrap around to -2147483648, with no warning.

concepts.anchor: Like a form you fill in and hand back: writing on your copy changes nothing upstairs, but if they gave you the original folder, your notes are in it.
concepts.explain: Assigning to a variable name inside a function moves only the function’s own name, and the code that called it never sees that. Changing the object itself in place changes the one object both of them hold. Otherwise the only way out is return.

concepts.anchor: Like thirds in decimal: 0.333… never closes, however many digits you write.
concepts.explain: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so their sum is slightly above 0.3 and == returns False. Hold money in whole cents, or in Decimal.

parts.goal: Say what a function can change and what it hands back, and read where Python says code stopped.
Answer a few questions on what you have learned so far, from memory.

parts.brief: An agent wrote this function from one sentence: “apply the discounts to a price”. Called three times with the same price, it printed 90.0, then 81.0, then 72.9.
questions: Before you read it: someone asks for “apply the discounts to a price”. What has to be true of the answer, and what would you want to see to believe it?
Still before you open it: what could make three calls with the same price give three different answers?
Now walk through it. Name the line that makes the second call different from the first, and say what type you would store the price in instead of a float.
looks_for: A price with the discounts applied, and the same price in gives the same price out — calling it twice must not change anything.
Something is being kept from one call to the next: a list or a total that lives outside any single call and is added to each time. Code like this can carry what earlier calls did into later ones.

The default list is made once, when the function is defined, and discounts.append(0.1) adds to that same list on every call that does not pass its own — that is the line. And the price is a float: these three happen to come out clean, but money belongs in whole cents or Decimal, and other prices will not: 1.10 comes back as 0.9900000000000001.
parts.goal: Find why the same call gives a different answer the second time.
parts.target_note: discounts=[] in the first line is a default: the value the function uses when a call does not pass its own.
